title: How to Revise Your Entire JEE/NEET Syllabus in the Last 30 Days
description: With 30 days left, there's no time to re-study everything at first-pass depth. A week-by-week calendar for the final month, how to triage chapters by confidence, and separate subject splits for JEE and NEET.
author: Studyloaf Team

content.body: By the time you're 30 days out, you've covered the syllabus once. The most common mistake in this window is re-studying everything at first-pass depth: rereading whole chapters and redoing every example as if there were months left. There aren't. The last 30 days aren't for learning. They're for triage, timed practice, and arriving at the exam rested. Below is the method, a week-by-week calendar, and how the subject split differs between JEE and NEET.

content.heading: Step 1: Sort every chapter into two piles
content.body: Use your recent mock results, not your feelings about a chapter, to sort honestly. A chapter you like isn't the same as one you consistently score well on.

list: Confident: you'd get most questions right with a quick formula glance. These get one fast pass: formula sheet, key results, one worked example to check the method hasn't gone stale
Shaky: you'd have to work through the logic, and your mocks show you dropping marks there. These get a full worked-example pass and a timed problem set
Most students have more confident chapters than shaky ones by now, so this split alone usually cuts the month's workload by close to half

content.heading: Step 2: The 30-day calendar
content.body: Every week has the same rhythm: six days of targeted work and one full mock with a proper review. Mocks stop three days before the exam, so the final stretch is review and rest, not another timed ordeal.

table.caption: The final 30 days, week by week
rows: Shaky chapters, first half: full worked-example pass, one timed set per chapter
Full mock on day 7, then review
Shaky chapters, second half, plus a quick pass through confident chapters in your strongest subject
Full mock on day 14, then review
Mixed timed practice and previous years' papers; quick pass through the remaining confident chapters
Full mock on day 21, then review
Your error log and formula sheets; short timed sets on the chapters mocks keep exposing
Last full mock on day 26 or 27
Light review only: formula sheets, NCERT highlights, your top mistakes. Check your admit card, centre and route. Sleep on schedule

content.heading: A day in the final month
list: Morning, your best hours: one shaky chapter, worked examples then a timed set
Afternoon: practice or previous years' questions in a second subject
Evening: 30 to 45 minutes on your error log, rewriting each mistake as the rule you'll apply next time
Mock days: the full paper at the real exam time, then at least as long again reviewing it
Keep sleep fixed at the hours your exam needs. A 9 am JEE Main shift and a 2 pm NEET start call for different routines in the last fortnight

content.heading: How the split differs for JEE
content.body: JEE Main gives Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics 100 marks each, so there's no heavyweight subject to favour. Split the month by weakness instead: if your mocks show Mathematics trailing by 30 marks, it gets the largest share of shaky-chapter days. Numerical-answer questions have carried -1 for a wrong answer since 2022, so practise finishing calculations cleanly and leaving a numerical blank when you can't. If you're also sitting JEE Advanced, keep one multi-concept problem set a week in the plan, since Advanced questions chain topics in a way Main practice doesn't train.

content.heading: How the split differs for NEET
content.body: NEET gives Biology 360 of 720 marks, as much as Physics and Chemistry combined, so Biology should get roughly half of your revision days rather than a third. Most of that time is close NCERT rereading (diagrams, tables and the lines between the bold headings), because NEET Biology questions track NCERT closely. Physics and Chemistry time goes on problem practice, especially Physics numericals and Organic reactions, where rereading helps far less. Remember that from 2027 NEET is computer-based, so take at least your last two mocks on a screen.

content.heading: The mock mistake in both directions
content.body: Two opposite mistakes are equally common. One is stopping mocks entirely in the last month for fear a bad score will wreck your confidence; you lose the pacing practice you most need. The other is cramming a mock into the last day or two, when there's no time to act on it and it mostly adds anxiety. The middle path is the calendar above: one full mock a week, the last one about three days out.

content.heading: Common mistakes
list: Rereading confident chapters because it feels productive, while shaky ones wait
Splitting NEET days equally across three subjects when Biology is half the paper
Taking a mock but not reviewing it, which wastes most of its value
Changing sleep times in the final week instead of fixing them to your exam slot
Leaving admit card and centre checks to the night before

content.body: Once you've decided how many days each subject gets, Studyloaf's free timetable generator turns that into a day-by-day schedule from your subjects, hours per day and exam date, and the exam countdown shows exactly how many days you're working with.
